candidate.answerReason: For b≥1, an elementary comparison with integer powers of 10 gives 0≤log10(b)<b², forcing 0≤a<1, which is impossible. Thus a<0 and 0<b<1, so the ordered values are a<0<b<1<1/b.

methods.label: Locate b relative to 1, then order the values
methods.explanation:
We do not need the exact values of \(a\) and \(b\); we need their order. Since \(b^2>0\), the equation shows that \(a\) and \(\log_{10}b\) have the same sign. The key is to rule out \(b\ge1\).

Suppose \(b\ge1\). Choose a nonnegative integer \(n\) such that
\[
10^n\le b<10^{n+1}.
\]
The base-10 logarithm is increasing, so \(0\le\log_{10}b<n+1\). Also, \(100^n\ge n+1\): starting from \(1\), each of the \(n\) multiplications by \(100\) increases the running value by at least \(1\). Squaring \(b\ge10^n\) therefore gives
\[
0\le\log_{10}b<n+1\le100^n\le b^2.
\]
Divide the original equation by the positive number \(b^2\). The displayed bounds imply
\[
0\le a=\frac{\log_{10}b}{b^2}<1,
\]
which is impossible for a nonzero integer. This also excludes \(b=1\).

Hence \(0<b<1\), so \(\log_{10}b<0\) and therefore \(a<0\). Taking the reciprocal of \(0<b<1\) gives \(1/b>1\). Thus all five values are distinct and ordered as
\[
a<0<b<1<\frac1b.
\]
The median is the third value, \(b\), choice D.
